answer.rationale: Temporal evidence points at the release: degradation began ~90 minutes ago, the release shipped ~2 hours ago, and the impact is confined to the primary region rather than spread across regions the way a shared-dependency or capacity problem usually is. Rolling back removes the most likely cause instead of relocating its symptoms. The competing candidate, regional failover (memory_b2), is the option I most want to avoid committing to first: b2 records a March latency degradation that resolved cleanly, but if the true cause is code in the new build, failover carries the bad build into the secondary region while forcing a cutover of heavy in-flight settlement writes at daily peak. That is the specific way this plan loses customer writes, which the primary objective forbids. Capacity (b3) was validated against a predictable promotional surge, not a post-release latency cliff, and provisioning would not land inside the current window. Read-replica routing (b5) relieves read pressure on the primary, but the pain here is on the write path, so it addresses the wrong axis. Circuit breakers (b4) contained an external partner failure; there is no partner signal here, and failing fast on our own write path would shed exactly the settlement writes we are protecting. I chose to verify memory_b1 because it is the single record my intended action rests on, and its summary asserts two things I need to actually check rather than inherit: that the rollback caused the recovery rather than merely preceding it, and that the prior build is genuinely a safe landing point. A rollback summary is also the kind of record most likely to have been consolidated optimistically, since the incident ended well. The archived source should tell me whether day 18 involved schema or data-format migrations, because a forward-only migration in today's release would make rollback actively destructive to writes rather than neutral. I am running this as a small guarded rollback on a bounded slice of write-path nodes rather than a full fleet revert: it keeps the action reversible, and it produces a real causal read. If p99 recovers on the reverted slice while the untouched slice stays degraded, the release is confirmed and I escalate to full rollback in the same window. If both slices stay degraded, the release is likely not the cause and regional failover becomes the next candidate, with write-drain sequencing planned in advance. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: the release and the settlement peak coincide, so a latent inefficiency in the new build could be surfacing only under peak write load, which would mean rollback helps now but the defect returns at the next peak. I am also not assuming the primary-region confinement rules out an underlying regional infrastructure fault that the release merely made visible.
